decks.domain: Drinking, drugs and health: alcohol effects, BAC limits, breath-test refusal, impaired-driver signs, drugs and fitness to drive

cards.front: How can alcohol affect a driver's thinking, and does a small amount matter?
cards.back: Alcohol can make a driver overconfident and unable to think clearly, and even a small amount raises the chance of a crash, including when the driver believes they are under the legal limit.

cards.front: After how many drinks does alcohol start to impair driving skills, and which skills suffer?
cards.back: After two, three or four drinks, alcohol starts to impair reaction time, coordination and balance, and it also dulls vision and the ability to judge distance.
cards.memory_hook: two to four drinks dull everything

cards.front: What combination accounts for much of the reckless, aggressive driving behind fatal highway crashes?
cards.back: Alcohol paired with anger accounts for much of the reckless, aggressive driving behind fatal highway crashes.

cards.front: What kind of crash do most alcohol-related crashes involve, and who gets hurt?
cards.back: Most alcohol-related crashes involve a single vehicle, yet they often kill or seriously injure several people, including passengers, pedestrians and other drivers.

cards.front: What sobers a person up, and how does the body get rid of alcohol?
cards.back: Only time sobers a person up: the liver burns off about ninety percent of the alcohol and the other ten percent leaves through breath, urine and sweat, which is why quick sober-up tricks fail.

cards.front: How much alcohol do one and a half ounces of eighty-proof whiskey, twelve ounces of beer and five ounces of wine each hold?
cards.back: One and a half ounces of eighty-proof whiskey, twelve ounces of beer and five ounces of wine each hold about the same half ounce of alcohol.

cards.front: According to the studies the manual cites, what had most drivers arrested for drunk driving been drinking?
cards.back: According to the studies the manual cites, beer is what most drivers arrested for drunk driving had been drinking.

decks.module: BAC, legal limits and crash risk
decks.domain: Drinking, drugs and health: alcohol effects, BAC limits, breath-test refusal, impaired-driver signs, drugs and fitness to drive

cards.front: What is BAC, and how is it revealed?
cards.back: Blood alcohol concentration, or BAC, is the only scientific measure of how much is too much, and a simple breath test reveals it.

cards.front: What four factors does BAC depend on?
cards.back: BAC depends on four factors: how much alcohol was consumed, body weight, how quickly the drinks went down, and what food was eaten.

cards.front: What can food do about alcohol, and what can it not do?
cards.back: Food slows how fast alcohol enters the blood, but it cannot prevent a high BAC during steady heavy drinking and it does not make anyone sober.

cards.front: Can eating a big meal keep heavy drinking from producing a high BAC?
cards.back: Eating slows alcohol absorption, but heavy drinking always produces a high BAC whatever was eaten.

cards.front: What does New Jersey law make illegal about driving after drinking or drug use?
cards.back: New Jersey makes it illegal to drive while impaired by liquor or by narcotic, hallucinogenic or habit-forming drugs, and also to drive with a BAC at or above zero point zero eight percent.

cards.front: What BAC is illegal for a driver younger than twenty-one, and what penalties apply?
cards.back: For a driver younger than twenty-one, driving with a BAC of zero point zero one percent or higher is illegal and carries severe penalties on top of any DUI penalties.

cards.front: How does the adult BAC limit compare with the limit for a driver under twenty-one?
cards.back: The adult limit is a BAC of zero point zero eight percent, while a driver under twenty-one breaks the law at just zero point zero one percent.

cards.front: At what BAC does the risk of causing a crash double?
cards.back: At a BAC slightly above zero point zero five percent, the risk of causing a crash doubles.

cards.front: How much greater is crash risk at the higher BAC levels the manual names?
cards.back: Crash risk is six times as great at a BAC of zero point one zero percent and twenty-five times as great at zero point one five percent.

cards.front: How does crash risk climb as BAC rises through the three levels the manual gives?
cards.back: Crash risk roughly doubles just above zero point zero five percent BAC, climbs to six times at zero point one zero percent and to twenty-five times at zero point one five percent.

decks.domain: Drinking, drugs and health: alcohol effects, BAC limits, breath-test refusal, impaired-driver signs, drugs and fitness to drive

cards.front: Is refusing a breath test allowed in New Jersey, and what penalties can follow?
cards.back: Refusing a breath test is illegal in New Jersey, and penalties include losing driving privileges, referral to an Intoxicated Driver Resource Center (IDRC), fines and an ignition interlock device.

cards.front: What extra charge does a breath-test refusal bring, and what happens if it goes unpaid?
cards.back: A driver who refuses a breath test also owes a violation surcharge, and leaving it unpaid suspends driving privileges indefinitely until it is paid.

cards.front: What five telltale signs of a drinking driver are police trained to watch for?
cards.back: Police are trained to watch for five telltale signs of a drinking driver: speeding, weaving, unusually slow driving, jerky changes of speed and abrupt stops at signs or lights.

cards.front: Why can slow driving signal that a driver is impaired?
cards.back: Slow driving can also signal impairment, because an intoxicated driver may be overly cautious and fall below the normal flow of traffic.

cards.front: Can weaving show up when an intoxicated driver never leaves the lane?
cards.back: Weaving can show up even when an intoxicated driver stays inside the correct lane, because holding a straight line becomes hard.

cards.front: What do jerky driving and quick stops mean as signs of an intoxicated driver?
cards.back: Jerky driving means short mental lapses that keep an intoxicated driver from holding a steady speed on a clear road, and quick stops mean braking suddenly at a sign or light instead of easing up.

decks.domain: Drinking, drugs and health confusables and continuation details

cards.front: What is the surest way to avoid a drinking-and-driving crash, and what alternatives does the manual suggest?
cards.back: The surest way to avoid a drinking-and-driving crash is not to drive at all after drinking, and the manual suggests a designated driver, public transportation or a cab instead.

cards.front: What does a designated driver take responsibility for?
cards.back: A designated driver takes responsibility for getting friends or family who have been drinking home safely, which also protects other motorists.

cards.front: What did New Jersey do first among the states for designated drivers?
cards.back: New Jersey was the first state to officially launch the Hero Campaign for designated drivers.

cards.front: How does a good host handle drinks and food at a party?
cards.back: A good host offers alcohol-free drinks and nourishing food, never pushes drinks or refills, and stops serving alcohol well before the party ends.

cards.front: What should a host do when a guest has had too much to drink?
cards.back: If a guest has had too much, do not let them drive: suggest a nap or an overnight stay, call the police only as a last resort, and remember that a host can be sued over a guest's drunk-driving crash.

decks.domain: Drinking, drugs and health: alcohol effects, BAC limits, breath-test refusal, impaired-driver signs, drugs and fitness to drive

cards.front: What does New Jersey law say about drugs and driving?
cards.back: It is illegal to drive in New Jersey while under the influence of any drug, or while carrying any drug without a valid prescription.

cards.front: What must drivers using prescription drugs be able to show police, and how is a prescription drug treated without one?
cards.back: Drivers using prescription drugs must show proof of the prescription to police when asked, and a drug that requires a prescription is treated as illegal if the driver has none.

cards.front: What should you do about a medicine labeled as possibly causing drowsiness or dizziness, and which medicines can affect driving?
cards.back: Do not take a medicine labeled as possibly causing drowsiness or dizziness before driving; cold pills, tranquilizers and some prescription drugs can affect basic driving skills.

cards.front: What should you check before combining drugs, and what should you never mix with any drug?
cards.back: Never combine drugs without asking a medical professional about side effects and driving, and never mix alcohol with any drug or medication.

cards.front: Why should you ask a professional about an over-the-counter drug before driving?
cards.back: Ask a professional how an over-the-counter drug may affect driving, because legal medicines can still impair.

cards.front: After alcohol, which drug is most often found in drivers involved in crashes?
cards.back: After alcohol, marijuana is the drug most often found in drivers involved in crashes.

cards.front: Which driving abilities can marijuana weaken?
cards.back: Marijuana can weaken a driver's tracking (staying in the lane), distance judgment, vigilance and ability to divide attention among many tasks.

decks.domain: Drinking, drugs and health confusables and continuation details

cards.front: Can a minor health problem interfere with driving, and what should you do when you feel unwell?
cards.back: Any health problem, even a stiff neck, a cough or a sore leg, can interfere with driving, so let someone else drive when you feel unwell.

cards.front: How often should you have your eyes tested?
cards.back: Have your eyes tested every year or two, and every year once you are over age forty.

cards.front: What does state law allow the MVC to do with the driving population?
cards.back: State law allows the MVC to retest the driving population.

cards.front: What does good side vision let a driver do?
cards.back: Good side (peripheral) vision lets a driver notice things out of the corners of the eyes while still looking straight ahead.

cards.front: What is a frequent cause of crashes, and what should a driver always know?
cards.back: Poor distance judgment is a frequent cause of crashes, so a driver should always know how far the vehicle is from nearby objects.

cards.front: Why does hearing matter for drivers, and what should you avoid?
cards.back: Hearing matters because horns, sirens and screeching tires give warnings, so keep the radio low and never drive wearing earphones.

recap_hooks.text: Alcohol breeds overconfidence and clouds thinking, and after two, three or four drinks it dulls reaction time, balance, vision and distance judgment.
Time is the only cure: the liver burns off about ninety percent, the rest leaves through breath, urine and sweat, so tricks never sober anyone up.
Whiskey at one and a half ounces, beer at twelve ounces and wine at five ounces each hold about a half ounce of alcohol.

recaps.module: BAC, legal limits and crash risk

recap_hooks.text: BAC is the scientific measure a breath test reveals, and it depends on how much you drank, your weight, how fast you drank and what you ate.
In New Jersey the adult line is zero point zero eight percent, and a driver under twenty-one breaks the law at zero point zero one percent.
Crash risk doubles just above zero point zero five, reaches six times at zero point one zero and twenty-five times at zero point one five.
Saying no to a breath test is itself illegal, bringing lost privileges, an IDRC referral, fines, an ignition interlock and a surcharge that suspends driving if left unpaid.
Police watch for speeding, weaving, unusually slow driving, jerky speed changes and abrupt stops, and slow, careful-looking driving can still mean impairment.
The surest plan after drinking is not to drive at all: use a designated driver, public transportation or a cab.
A good host serves food and alcohol-free drinks, stops serving early, and keeps an overserved guest from driving with a nap or an overnight stay.
In New Jersey you may not drive under the influence of any drug or drive carrying one without a valid prescription, and you must show that prescription when police ask.
Skip any medicine that warns of drowsiness or dizziness before driving, ask a professional about over-the-counter drugs, and never mix alcohol with any drug.
Marijuana is the drug found most often in crash drivers after alcohol, and it can weaken lane tracking, distance judgment, vigilance and divided attention.
Even a stiff neck or a cough can get in the way of driving, so hand over the wheel when you feel unwell.
Get your eyes checked every year or two, and every year once you are over forty, and know that state law lets the MVC retest drivers.
Use your side vision, always know how far you are from nearby objects, and keep the radio low so you can hear horns and sirens.
